title: Which Tennessee Landlord-Tenant Law Applies Where
bodyText:
Tennessee's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies only in counties that had more than 75,000 people in the 2010 federal census, and in 2021 the legislature froze that list so later censuses do not change it.

The Act counties are Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson.

In the other 78 counties the Act does not apply: there is no statutory security-deposit procedure, late-fee cap, entry rule, retaliation ban, abandonment procedure or periodic-notice rule, and termination for a tenant's default follows a separate statute (14 days' notice for unpaid rent or damage, which the tenant can cure; 30 days for any other default; 3 days for violence, drug-related criminal activity or a threat to safety by a tenant who is not disabled; 3 days for an unauthorized occupant who refuses to leave).

Some rules apply in every county: domestic-violence lease termination, service and support animal rules, guide dog protections, the detainer (eviction) court process, squatter removal, the smoke alarm law, the $30 bounced-check charge, fair housing, the ban on local rent control and, from January 1, 2027, tenants' firearm rights.

In an Act county the Act also bars the county government from adding its own landlord-tenant regulations. Even in an Act county the Act does not cover institutional residence, occupancy under a contract to buy, transient lodging, condominium or co-op owners, agricultural leases, or public housing where federal rules conflict.

Choose the Act-county or other-county version of the paired lease clauses to match the county the property is in.

title: Tennessee Security Deposit Rules
bodyText:
In the 17 Act counties a landlord who takes a security deposit before occupancy must keep it in an account used only for deposits at a regulated bank or lending institution and must tell the tenant, when the lease is signed and the deposit paid, where the account is (not the account number).

At move-out the tenant has a right to be present at an inspection; if the landlord gives written notice of that right and the lease warns that a tenant who schedules and then misses the inspection waives any dispute, a no-show tenant cannot contest the damage found. The landlord must list the damage and estimated repair costs.

A landlord who did not use a separate account AND did not provide the damage list may not keep any of the deposit. Damage found later can be charged only if discovered within 30 days after the tenant left or 7 days after a new tenant moved in, whichever is earlier. If a refund is due, the landlord sends notice of the amount to the tenant's last known address; if the tenant does not respond within 60 days the landlord may keep it.

Tennessee sets no deadline for returning a deposit, no cap on its size and no interest requirement.

Outside the Act counties there is no deposit statute at all; the lease governs. On a good-faith sale, the seller is released once the deposit is transferred to the buyer and the tenant is notified in writing.

title: No Limit on Security Deposit Amount
bodyText: Tennessee does not limit the amount of a security deposit, pet deposit or prepaid rent a landlord may require, in any county.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: Tennessee does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit. In the 17 Act counties the deposit must be in a separate account used only for deposits, but the law says nothing about interest.

title: Late Fees in Tennessee
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a late fee cannot be charged until a five-day grace period has run, counting the day rent was due; if the last grace day is a Sunday or a legal holiday (including an election day), rent paid the next business day is on time; and any late charge, however it is labeled, is capped at 10% of the rent past due. Outside the Act counties Tennessee has no late-fee statute: there is no grace period and no cap, and the fee is a lease term that a court can refuse to enforce if it is a penalty rather than a reasonable estimate of the landlord's loss. Many landlords in non-Act counties follow the 10% and five-day limits anyway.

title: No Application Fee Limit
bodyText: Tennessee does not limit rental application or screening fees, and no statute requires a refund of an unused fee.

title: Bounced Checks
bodyText: When a check, draft or order is returned for no account, insufficient funds or a bad signature, the payee may charge a handling fee of up to $30. Separately, a person who writes a bad check with fraudulent intent can be liable in a civil action for the check, 10% interest, reasonable service charges, court costs and attorney's fees, unless they pay in full within 10 days after notice of dishonor; if they still do not pay within 30 days after a certified-mail notice that treble damages will be sought, the court awards treble the check amount, with the extra capped at $500. No statute sets a fee for a failed electronic or card payment.

title: Local Rent Control and Housing Mandates Preempted
bodyText: No city or county in Tennessee may control the amount of rent for private residential or commercial property, or require private rental units to be rented or sold below market rate (including as a condition of a zoning change, variance, permit or development approval); only voluntary incentive programs are allowed, and a person who loses money because of a prohibited local rule may sue for actual damages. In the 17 Act counties the Act also occupies the whole field of landlord-tenant regulation and bars the county government from adding to it. Other local rules still exist and are outside this library's state-level scope: Metro Nashville landlord registration, rental inspection districts, short-term rental ordinances, towing and code enforcement.

title: No Rent Increase Notice Rule
bodyText: Tennessee sets no notice period or limit for rent increases. A month-to-month rent change takes effect by ending the tenancy with the required notice and offering new terms. In the 17 Act counties a landlord may not raise rent in retaliation for a tenant's complaint or use of the Act's remedies, and a landlord converting a rental unit to a condominium in certain counties must let the tenant keep renting at the same rate for two months.

title: No Rent Receipt Duty
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to give a receipt for rent paid in cash or otherwise.

title: Termination Notices for Tenant Default
bodyText: ACT COUNTIES: for a material breach, or a breach of the tenant's health-and-safety duties, the landlord gives written notice describing the breach; if it can be fixed by paying rent, repairs, damages or another amount, the tenant has 14 days after receiving the notice to fix it (tenant repairs need the landlord's prior written approval, and the notice must say so); if substantially the same breach recurs within six months the landlord may terminate on 7 days' written notice; if the breach cannot be fixed, the lease ends on a date at least 14 days after the notice. A tenant can waive the nonpayment notice in 12-point bold lease text. For violence, a real and present danger to health or safety, a hazardous or unsanitary condition, or an unauthorized occupant who refuses to leave, the landlord may terminate 3 days after the tenant receives written notice, and the tenant may go straight to court to challenge it. A week-to-week tenancy ends on 10 days' written notice and a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' notice before a rent date. OTHER COUNTIES: 14 days' notice for unpaid rent due and in arrears after demand, or for damage beyond normal wear and tear, and the lease does not end if the tenant cures before the date in the notice (a repeat within six months allows termination on 14 days' notice); 30 days' notice for any other default; 3 days' notice for violence, drug-related criminal activity or a threat to safety by a tenant who is not mentally or physically disabled; 3 days for an unauthorized subtenant or occupant who refuses to leave. These rules do not apply to rental periods under 14 days, and no statute sets a periodic-tenancy notice outside the Act. EVERY COUNTY: public housing authority tenants can be terminated on 3 days' notice for the same serious conduct; a 55-and-over federally assisted elderly facility must give 60 days' notice to a paid-up tenant before evicting for redevelopment; and a district attorney may bring an eviction where premises are knowingly used for drug or prostitution offenses. Where the tenant signed the bold waiver of the nonpayment notice, or a repeat breach lets you terminate without a new chance to cure, the lease doesn't require a further written notice of the default; you may still give one first.

title: Eviction (Detainer) Process
bodyText:
After the required termination notice, the landlord files a detainer warrant in general sessions court (or circuit court).

The summons may be served on any adult in possession, by certified mail through the sheriff or constable, on a party the lease names for service, or, after three documented failed personal-service attempts, by posting on the door and first-class mail at least six days before the hearing. Trial is at least six days after service, and may be postponed only up to seven days on request. The judge decides possession and rent, interest and damages.

No writ of possession issues until 10 days after judgment, and a tenant who appeals must post a bond or cash deposit of one year's rent.

When the officer removes the tenant, the landlord places the tenant's belongings on the premises clear of the entrance and away from the road and must leave them undisturbed for 48 hours, after which they may be discarded; the landlord is not liable for damage to them unless malicious.

Since 2026, a private party serving or executing eviction papers may not live-stream or broadcast video of it to the public without the person's written consent, with statutory damages of at least $25,000 per intentional violation; sharing it with the landlord, owner, their lawyer, the manager, the court or police is allowed.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: A landlord may not take possession by changing locks, removing the tenant's belongings, or shutting off utilities or other essential services; possession comes only through the court process, or after abandonment or surrender. In the 17 Act counties a tenant who is unlawfully removed or excluded, or whose essential services are willfully cut, may recover possession or end the lease, and recover actual damages, punitive damages where appropriate, and attorney's fees, plus prepaid rent and the deposit. In every county, entering and holding property by force, threats or putting a person's goods out of doors is a forcible entry and detainer the occupant can sue over, and property may be entered only where the law allows and then only peaceably.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a landlord may not raise rent, reduce services, or bring or threaten an eviction because the tenant complained to the landlord of a violation or used a remedy under the Act. The landlord may still evict if the code problem was caused mainly by the tenant's household or guests, if the tenant is behind on rent, or if code compliance requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit. Outside the Act counties no statute prohibits retaliation.

title: Holdover Remedies
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, if a tenant stays without consent after the lease ends, the landlord may sue for possession, back rent, reasonable attorney's fees and any other damages the lease provides for, and, if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, actual damages and fees as well. If the landlord consents to the tenant staying, the tenant pays the reasonable value of use and occupancy. Outside the Act counties no statute sets a holdover measure; the landlord uses the detainer process and the lease.

title: Domestic Abuse: Evicting Only the Perpetrator
bodyText: If domestic abuse is the reason a tenancy is being terminated, only the perpetrator may be evicted; the landlord may not evict the victims, children under 18 or innocent occupants solely because of the abuse, and the perpetrator stays liable for all amounts due under the lease. The landlord may remove the perpetrator from the lease and require the remaining adults to qualify for a new lease for the rest of the term, and is not liable to the perpetrator for doing so. The victim and all adult tenants must agree in writing not to let the perpetrator return and to report any return, and breaking that agreement is cause to terminate. These protections apply only after the victim obtains an order of protection for the specific incident that orders the perpetrator out or away, or finds a danger, and gives the landlord a copy; they do not apply where the perpetrator is a child or dependent of a tenant, and they do not stop an eviction of a victim for nonpayment or other lease violations. Separately, a tenant who is a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking may end the lease early with documentation.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: Tennessee has no state statute letting a servicemember end a residential lease; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act governs, and the lease's early-termination terms preserve it.

title: Lease Termination for Public Housing Acceptance (Physical Disability)
bodyText: A tenant who is permanently and totally disabled with a physical disability may end a lease of their primary residence, without penalty or rent after moving out, when accepted into a public housing facility, by giving the landlord written proof of the acceptance; the landlord must acknowledge the termination in writing. The right does not apply if the landlord has made significant accessibility modifications to the unit for a person with a physical disability.

title: Drug and Prostitution Activity at Rental Property
bodyText: A tenancy may be terminated where the premises or the area immediately around them is knowingly used for prostitution-related or drug-sale offenses. The district attorney can demand in writing that the owner or landlord commit, within five days, to diligently seek the eviction; if the landlord does not, or does not follow through, the district attorney may bring the eviction as if they were the landlord, can recover fees and costs from the respondents, and the landlord pays the cost of removing the tenant's belongings (up to $200). Real property used repeatedly for serious drug offenses can also be forfeited to the state.

title: Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Since 2024 a property owner or authorized agent can ask the county sheriff to remove a person unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling without going to court, using a sworn complaint in the statutory form, if the person entered unlawfully, the property was not open to the public, the owner told them to leave, they are not a current or former tenant under any written or oral lease the owner authorized, they are not the owner's immediate family, and no related lawsuit is pending. The sheriff serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts the owner in possession. False or wrongful use exposes the owner to actual damages, statutory damages of three times fair market rent, costs and fees. It cannot be used against a tenant or former tenant; they must be evicted through the court. For an unauthorized subtenant or occupant who came in through a tenant, the landlord may terminate on 3 days' notice (both regimes). A 2025 law gives a similar remedy for commercial property.

title: No Lease Termination on a Tenant's Death
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute ending a lease when a tenant dies or setting a procedure for a deceased tenant's belongings. In the 17 Act counties the landlord may enter the unit if the tenant is deceased, incapacitated or incarcerated.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute sealing, expunging or limiting public access to eviction (detainer) case records.

title: Selling a Rented Property
bodyText: A lease binds a buyer of rented property. In the 17 Act counties a landlord who sells in good faith to a bona fide buyer is released from liability under the lease for events after the tenant receives written notice of the sale and the deposit is transferred to the buyer, and the owner-disclosure information must be kept current by the successor. Tennessee has no statute protecting tenants when the landlord's lender forecloses; the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act applies.

title: No State Foreclosure Protection for Tenants
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute giving tenants notice or other rights when the landlord's lender forecloses. The federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act generally lets a bona fide tenant stay to the end of the lease, or at least 90 days after notice.

title: Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies
bodyText:
In the 17 Act counties the landlord must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, make all repairs needed to keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, and in complexes of four or more units provide trash receptacles.

A tenant may recover damages, get an injunction and recover attorney's fees after giving 14 days' written notice of the landlord's noncompliance.

If the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply essential services (utilities such as gas, heat and electricity, and other duties materially affecting health and safety), the tenant, after written notice, may buy the service and deduct the cost from rent, recover the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and pay no rent meanwhile, plus fees.

Tenants must keep their part of the premises clean and safe, dispose of waste, not damage the property or engage in illegal conduct, and not disturb neighbors; if a tenant fails a health-and-safety duty that can be fixed, the landlord may do the work after 14 days' written notice and bill it as rent.

Outside the Act counties there is no statutory repair duty or repair remedy; the lease and local housing codes govern.

title: Lease Terms Tennessee Voids
bodyText:
In the 17 Act counties a lease may not have the tenant confess judgment, exculpate or limit the landlord's liability arising under law, or indemnify the landlord for it; such terms are unenforceable, and a landlord who willfully uses a lease containing terms known to be prohibited is liable to the tenant for actual damages. A lease also cannot make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act, and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable term.

A contractual lien on a tenant's household goods is unenforceable unless perfected by a UCC filing with the Secretary of State, and every other landlord lien is prohibited.

Outside the Act counties these rules do not apply, and an old statute still allows a lease bond in which the tenant authorizes a confessed judgment for possession at the end of the term, though a general statute voids pre-suit confessions of judgment and how the two fit is unresolved; the library offers it only as an optional clause for those counties, and offers an optional perfected household-goods security interest for the Act counties. The library's parking, storage, insurance and pet clauses avoid exculpatory and indemnity language in every county.

title: Rules and Regulations
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a landlord's rule is enforceable only if it promotes tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects the property from abusive use or fairly distributes services; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies to all tenants; is explicit enough to tell tenants what to do; is not meant to evade the landlord's duties; and the tenant had notice of it when signing. A rule adopted later binds the tenant if reasonable notice is given and it does not substantially modify the lease. From January 1, 2027, a rule is also unenforceable if it violates tenants' firearm rights.

title: Tenant Firearm Rights (from 2027)
bodyText:
For leases entered into, amended, extended or renewed on or after January 1, 2027, a Tennessee landlord may not prohibit a tenant's lawful possession, carrying, transport or storage of firearms, firearm parts or ammunition in the unit, in a vehicle in tenant parking, or in other areas the landlord controls on the way between them.

The landlord may require firearms to be concealed, holstered or in a carrying container when moved between vehicle and unit and in common areas, and for noncompliance may ask the tenant to comply and use any other remedy the lease expressly states, so long as it does not bar lawful possession in the unit. A tenant can sue for an injunction, actual and punitive damages and attorney's fees.

Some facilities are excluded (state-agency leases, licensed mental health, children's services, hospital, nursing and assisted-care facilities, certain independent living, and school property).

Remove any firearm ban from leases and rules signed or renewed from 2027. Separately, handgun permit holders may keep a firearm locked in their vehicle in a parking area under existing law.

title: Electronic Notices
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, if the tenant provides an e-mail address in the lease, the landlord may send notices required by the Act to it unless a section requires another form (for example posting and mailing for abandonment, or a certificate of mailing for a deposit damage list); a landlord may not require an e-mail address as a condition of renting. Tennessee's electronic transactions law has no exclusion for eviction or default notices, so in any county parties who agree to transact electronically can use e-mail for written notices, though court papers are served under the detainer statute.

title: Landlord Registration (Metro Nashville / Davidson County)
bodyText: In a county with a metropolitan government and more than 500,000 people (Davidson County, Metro Nashville), every landlord of one or more dwelling units must file with the local building-codes agency the landlord's or agent's name, phone and street address (not a P.O. box) and the address of each unit, on the agency's form, with a fee of up to $10 a year, and must report changes of ownership within 30 days. Failure is fined $50 per week after a hearing on at least 15 days' mailed notice. If you own through an out-of-state LLC or corporation, it must get a certificate of authority from the Secretary of State before transacting business in Tennessee, and until it does it may not maintain an eviction or other court case (its contracts stay valid and it may defend a case); it also owes a fine or back fees for the years it went without (Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 48-249-904(a), 48-249-913, 48-25-101, 48-25-102). Owning property, without more, is not transacting business, but the law treats managing and renting real property as outside that rule only when the property came through a foreclosure and is being sold off, so register before you rent (Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 48-249-902(a)(9), 48-25-101(b)(9)). An unregistered LLC that transacts business here can be served through the Secretary of State (Tenn. Code Ann. § 48-249-112(b)). A corporation must file an assumed-name application before doing business under any other name (Tenn. Code Ann. § 48-14-101(d)(3)).

title: Rental Inspection Districts and Code-Violation Inspections
bodyText: State law lets Metro Nashville and certain cities (identified by population bracket) create residential rental inspection districts in deteriorating areas, with owner notification, initial and periodic inspections, fees and penalties; the Act's landlord-tenant rights are unchanged. Separately, any Tennessee city may inspect inside a rental unit that has had three code violations cited on three different dates within six months, with the tenant's consent, a warrant or in an emergency.

title: Water and Wastewater Tenant Form (Hamilton County)
bodyText: In Hamilton County, a water and wastewater authority must provide a written acknowledgment form that a tenant completes when entering into or renewing a residential lease (where the unit is not submetered or billed by allocation). The landlord must send the completed form to the authority within one business day; once it does, the authority cannot collect the tenant's delinquent charges from the landlord or a later tenant. A landlord may refuse to rent to an applicant who will not complete it, but a landlord who rents to one who did not complete it is liable for that tenant's unpaid charges. The authority may require a deposit of up to three months' average charges on the tenant's first bill.

title: Cooperating with Child Abuse Investigations
bodyText: A landlord or person in control of residential rental property must give a Department of Children's Services case manager or child protective investigation team information, if known, about the address or location of a child alleged to be abused or neglected who lives or is located on the property, and is not liable for cooperating. Separately, Tennessee makes every person a reporter: anyone who knows of harm to a child that reasonably appears to come from brutality, abuse or neglect must report it immediately to the juvenile judge, the Department of Children's Services, the sheriff or the city's chief law enforcement officer, and anyone who knows or reasonably suspects that a child has been sexually abused must report it to the Department (Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 37-1-403(a), 37-1-605(a)). Knowingly failing to report is a Class A misdemeanor, a second failure is a Class E felony, and an intentional failure is a Class E felony (Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 37-1-412(a), 37-1-615(a)).

title: Tennessee Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Tennessee's Human Rights Act bars housing discrimination because of race, color, creed, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin - the federal classes plus creed. It covers refusing to rent or negotiate, discriminatory terms, false statements of unavailability, and discriminatory ads, application forms and records of inquiry; for disability it requires reasonable accommodations and, at the tenant's expense, reasonable modifications (a landlord may require restoration of the interior at move-out), and accessible design for covered multifamily buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991. Exemptions include an owner-occupied building of two units, renting a single room in one's own residence, certain religious organizations, and single-sex dormitories; housing for older persons is exempt from familial status. Tennessee has no source-of-income, sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status or military status class. Separately, a physically disabled person must be given priority for first- and second-floor units in rental buildings of three or more stories where the disability would prevent reasonable access to higher floors (a Class C misdemeanor, $50 fine).

title: No Source-of-Income Protection
bodyText: Tennessee law does not require landlords to accept housing choice vouchers or protect source of income, and local governments cannot impose below-market rental mandates.

title: Service and Support Animal Law
bodyText: Tennessee's statute on service and support animals in rentals applies in every county. A landlord may ask for reliable documentation only when the disability or the need is not apparent, may verify it without seeking medical records, and may deny a request if documentation is not provided; website certificates sold for a fee are not reliable documentation. A tenant who misrepresents a disability or need, or supplies false documentation, commits a material lease default, and knowingly doing so is also a crime. A landlord is not liable for injuries caused by an animal allowed as a reasonable accommodation. A legally blind tenant's guide dog cannot carry a deposit, and refusing to rent to a blind person because of a guide dog is a misdemeanor. Federal fair housing law still applies.

title: Renting to Applicants with Criminal Records
bodyText: Since 2021 a landlord cannot be held liable for negligence solely because it rented to a person with a prior criminal conviction, and evidence of that conviction is not admissible in such a suit, unless the landlord actually knew of a conviction for a violent offense or violent sexual offense, or learned of one committed during the tenancy and willfully let the person stay. Tennessee has no statute limiting the use of criminal history or credit reports in screening; federal fair housing and consumer-reporting laws apply.

title: Immigration Status and the 2025 Harboring Law
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring or forbidding a landlord to ask about immigration status. In 2025 Tennessee made human smuggling a felony, including intentionally concealing, harboring or shielding from detection, for commercial advantage or private gain, a person the defendant knows has illegally entered or remained in the United States; 'harbor' is defined as providing shelter to or concealing the whereabouts of such a person. The law imposes no duty to check status, and this library has not researched whether an ordinary lease could fall within it; ask counsel before relying on either reading. Screening by national origin or apparent citizenship risks a fair housing violation.

title: Methamphetamine Lab Quarantine and Reporting
bodyText: Local law enforcement may quarantine property where methamphetamine was made, post it, record a notice with the register of deeds and notify owners and lienholders. It is a Class B misdemeanor to offer quarantined property for habitation or to live in it, and the quarantine stays until a certified industrial hygienist certifies the property safe (a certificate of fitness can be recorded). A landlord, manager or agent of property they do not live in who knows or reasonably should know meth is or was manufactured there must notify law enforcement within 24 hours (Class B misdemeanor). There is no statute requiring a landlord to disclose a past meth lab to a new tenant.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to test for or disclose radon.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose bed bugs or setting a treatment timeline. In the 17 Act counties the general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable applies.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose mold or setting a treatment timeline. In the 17 Act counties the general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable applies.

title: No Carbon Monoxide Alarm Duty for Rentals
bodyText: Tennessee's carbon monoxide alarm statute covers hotels and similar lodging with fuel-burning appliances, not apartments or rental houses; newer buildings follow the building code the state adopts. Smoke alarms are required.

title: Lead Paint: State Abatement Certification
bodyText: The federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to pre-1978 housing. Tennessee adds a certification program: after its rules took effect, lead-based paint inspection, risk assessment and abatement may be done only by certified persons, except an owner abating their own residential property, or routine cleaning and repainting by an owner or a property management company's employee where existing lead paint is not significantly damaged. Renovators of target housing must follow the state rules.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose flood risk, flood zone status or past flooding to a tenant.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to notify tenants about registered sex offenders nearby or in the building.

title: Condominium Conversion
bodyText: In Class 1 and Class 2 counties (a population classification in the county-salary statute), an owner converting an occupied rental unit to a condominium or other unit for sale must give each tenant at least two months' actual notice and let the tenant keep renting at the same rate for those two months, even past the lease end; a sale to anyone else is invalid without that notice, a tenant who did not get it may stay two months at the same rent or leave immediately with reasonable moving expenses paid, and a tenant who must sue recovers costs and attorney's fees. Statewide, a condominium declarant must give residential tenants of a conversion building notice at least 60 days before they must vacate.

title: Towing from Rental Property
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a landlord may tow a vehicle not registered to a tenant, occupant or known guest that has been on the property more than seven consecutive days after posting 10 days' written notice on it; may tow immediately, without notice, a vehicle violating posted permit-parking or traffic and parking signs (fire lanes, hydrants, accessible spaces, trash receptacles); may tow flat-tired, inoperable, badly damaged or unregistered vehicles after 10 days' posted notice (the tow operator notifies police first if the owner is absent); and may tow a nuisance vehicle after 24 hours' posted notice. Outside the Act counties no statute gives landlords a towing procedure; cities may regulate towing, and moving a vehicle whose owner holds a lease interest in the property without consent is unlawful except on the owner's or tenant's request or by court order.

title: No Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a move-in inspection, condition checklist or inventory. The Act's inspection right is at move-out, in the 17 Act counties only.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Tennessee gives tenants no statutory right to install electric vehicle charging, satellite dishes or antennas.

title: No Tenant Flag Display Statute
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute protecting a tenant's display of the United States flag or other flags at a rental property.

title: No Limit on Pet Deposits or Pet Fees
bodyText: Tennessee does not limit pet deposits, pet rent or pet fees, except that no deposit or extra charge may be taken for a legally blind tenant's guide dog, and no pet payment for a service or support animal allowed as an accommodation.

title: No Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute protecting a tenant from eviction or penalty for calling police or emergency services, and no statute limiting nuisance ordinances that count such calls. In the 17 Act counties, general retaliation protection covers only complaints to the landlord and use of the Act's remedies.

title: No Duty to Disclose a Death, Crime or Non-Transmissible Illness
bodyText: No cause of action arises against a property owner for failing to disclose that an occupant had HIV or another disease medically determined to be highly unlikely to be transmitted by occupying a dwelling, or that the property was the site of a homicide, felony or suicide, or of an event that did not affect the physical property. Fair housing law separately bars treating an applicant differently because of a disability such as HIV.

title: Domestic Abuse, Sexual Assault or Stalking: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: For a lease entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2021, a tenant who, or whose household family member, is a domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking victim may end the lease with written notice requesting release, a mutually agreed release date within 30 days, and either an order of protection issued or extended after a hearing finding them a victim, or documentation of a criminal charge based on a police report, dated no more than 60 days before the notice (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-28-205 in the 17 Act counties; the same rule is Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-112 in every county). The tenant moves out within 30 days of notice or as agreed and owes rent for the full month in which the tenancy ends and outstanding obligations, but no future rent, penalty or fee; other parties aren't released. Don't reveal information that could locate the tenant without written consent unless law or a court requires it, and don't terminate or evict solely because of victim status. See also the note on evicting only the perpetrator.

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText:
Tennessee has two casualty rules, depending on the county. In the 17 counties where Tennessee's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-28-102(a)), if fire or casualty damages the property so that its use is substantially impaired, which the Act defines as a governmental authority having deemed it unfit for human habitation (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-28-104(15)), the tenant may move out immediately and tell you in writing within 14 days that they are ending the lease, which then ends on the date they moved out (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-28-503).

If the lease ends, return all prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit, accounting for rent as of the date the tenant returned the keys or moved out, whichever is earlier. That termination right does not exclude damage the tenant caused; the lease's tenant-caused damage clause preserves your claim for lost rent.

In the other 78 counties, if the building is destroyed or so damaged, by the elements or any other cause, that it is untenantable and unfit for occupancy, a tenant who was not at fault or negligent may surrender possession and owes no rent after surrendering, unless an express written agreement provides otherwise (Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-102(a)). The lease's casualty clause is written to satisfy both rules.

title: Ending a Month-to-Month or Week-to-Week Tenancy
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, a month-to-month tenancy ends on written notice given at least 30 days before the periodic rental date named as the end date, and a week-to-week tenancy on at least 10 days' written notice before the end date (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-512(a)-(b)). Outside the Act counties no statute sets a notice period for ending a periodic tenancy: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-7-109 sets notices only for ending a tenancy because of the tenant's default, and does not apply at all to rental periods under 14 days. Your lease states your chosen periods; the Act-county periods are a safe floor in every county.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule in either the 17 Act counties or the other 78: a landlord may decline to renew a fixed-term lease, or end a periodic tenancy with the required notice, without giving a reason. Limits that apply only in particular situations: in the Act counties a landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for a complaint about a violation of the deposit section or for using the Act's remedies; in every county a tenant may not be evicted solely because they are a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking, and a federally assisted 55-and-over elderly facility must give a paid-up tenant 60 days' notice before evicting for redevelopment; in Class 1 and Class 2 counties an owner converting an occupied unit to a condominium must give two months' notice at the same rent; and fair housing law applies everywhere. Tennessee has no rent-escrow bar on eviction and no statute protecting tenants' associations.

title: Tenant's Belongings and Animals After an Eviction
bodyText: When the officer removes the tenant under a detainer judgment, you or your representative must place the tenant's personal property on the premises, in an area clear of the entrance and a reasonable distance from any road, and must not disturb it for 48 hours; after that you may discard what remains. Local government action on the property is suspended during those 48 hours. If you follow this procedure you are not liable for damage to the property unless it is shown by clear and convincing evidence that the damage came from your malicious act or omission. Tennessee has no separate rule for animals left behind after an eviction. A person removed by a detainer who again illegally takes possession commits a Class C misdemeanor. In the 17 Act counties, belongings left after an abandonment (not an eviction) follow the separate abandonment procedure instead.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: Tennessee has no plain-language or readability statute for residential leases or consumer contracts generally; its readability tests are for insurance policies.

title: Tennessee Consumer Protection Act and Rentals
bodyText: The Tennessee Consumer Protection Act of 1977 defines trade, commerce and consumer transaction to include the lease or rental of property, real, personal or mixed, so its prohibitions can reach how a landlord advertises, offers and rents a home. None of its exemptions covers landlords as a group. It does exempt conduct that a state or federal law or rule specifically requires or authorizes, and a landlord who claims that exemption has to prove it. It prescribes no lease wording, no statement of waivers and no readability standard.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on landlords sharing rent data. Federal and state antitrust and consumer-protection law still apply.

title: Fees Count as Rent in the Act Counties
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, 'rent' means all payments the tenant must make to the landlord under the rental agreement, so a fee the lease requires is rent under the Act. That matters for any rule that turns on rent, such as the nonpayment notice and the late-fee cap measured on the rent past due. Outside the Act counties no statute defines rent, so the lease's own terms decide.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring every blank in a written lease to be completed or making an incomplete lease a breach. Completing every blank is still good practice.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute stating a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment for residential leases. In the 17 Act counties the tenant's possession is protected by the remedies for unlawful ouster and interrupted essential services and by the limits on landlord entry; elsewhere case law governs.

title: Forms Tennessee Law Supplies
bodyText: Tennessee statutes supply several forms: the detainer warrant, the judgment for possession and the writ of possession used in an eviction; the sworn complaint an owner files with the sheriff to remove an unlawful occupant, which must be substantially in the statutory form; and, in the 17 Act counties, the required contents of the abandonment notice a landlord posts and mails. In Hamilton County the water and wastewater authority supplies a tenant acknowledgment form. No statute prescribes a lease form.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: Tennessee has no landlord-tenant statute on tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells; the lease's alterations and rules terms govern. The general criminal wiretapping and surveillance law still applies to any recording.

title: Attorney's Fees in Tennessee Leases
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees for the tenant's breach of contract and nonpayment of rent only as the lease provides, and the Act separately awards fees to a landlord who terminates the lease, a holdover without consent, a refusal of lawful access, or a tenant's misrepresented need for a service or support animal. The Act gives the tenant fees for the landlord's noncompliance, failure to supply essential services, unlawful ouster, abusive entry and a bad-faith violence termination. The Act's fee awards are for reasonable fees, and no Tennessee statute requires a lease fee clause to be reciprocal. Outside the Act counties no statute awards fees in an ordinary eviction or rent case, so the landlord's fee claim rests on the lease's own fee clause. The library's Default by Tenant clause carries the fee term.

title: Collection Agency Fees
bodyText: No Tennessee landlord-tenant statute lets a lease add a collection agency's fee to what the tenant owes, or bars one. Collection agencies are licensed and regulated separately, and federal law limits what a third-party collector may add to a debt. In the 17 Act counties every payment the lease requires is rent, so a collection fee the lease imposes counts as rent for the Act's rules that turn on rent. A landlord who wants to pass on collection costs should state the fee, how it is calculated and when it applies in the lease, keep it to the agency's actual reasonable charge, and take advice first.

title: Fees for Serving Notices
bodyText: No Tennessee statute authorizes or bars a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice, or for filing an eviction. In the 17 Act counties any charge or fee, however it is labeled, that a landlord charges because rent was paid late counts toward the 10% late-fee cap, so a notice fee triggered by late rent must fit inside that cap together with the late fee. Court costs in an eviction are awarded by the court, not by a lease charge. A fixed fee that is not tied to the landlord's actual cost may be challenged as a penalty under case law.

title: Eviction Fee Clauses
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute banning a lease clause that charges the tenant a fee for being evicted. In the 17 Act counties the landlord who terminates may claim possession, rent, actual damages for the breach and reasonable attorney's fees, and any charge triggered by late rent counts toward the 10% late-fee cap. Outside the Act counties the court awards rent, interest and damages in the eviction. A flat eviction fee that is not tied to the landlord's actual loss risks being treated as a penalty under case law, so the library recovers actual costs and fees instead.

title: Liquidated Damages in Leases
bodyText: Tennessee has no general statute on liquidated damages in a residential lease; the UCC's liquidated-damages rules cover sales and leases of goods, not of homes. Whether a fixed sum for a breach (such as an early-termination fee) is enforceable is a question for case law; a fixed sum that is not tied to a genuine estimate of the landlord's loss risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty. In the 17 Act counties the landlord must also mitigate, and any charge for late rent counts toward the 10% late-fee cap. Take advice before relying on a fixed damages figure.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Charges
bodyText: A lease may set an interest rate on unpaid rent and charges, but Tennessee caps contract interest: for a written contract signed by the tenant the maximum is the state's applicable formula rate, and for other transactions 10% a year. When the landlord gets a judgment, the judgment bears the rate the lease fixes within those limits; otherwise it bears the court rate, two points below the published formula rate. In an eviction the general sessions judge decides the rent arrearage, interest and damages. In the 17 Act counties interest charged because rent is late may count toward the 10% late-fee cap, so the cautious course there is to keep interest and late fees together within that cap.

title: Time Limits for Suing
bodyText: In Tennessee an action for rent, or for the use and occupation of land, must be brought within six years after the claim arose, and the same six years applies to actions on contracts not covered by a more specific limit. In the 17 Act counties a tenant who disputes the landlord's final deposit damage list may sue in circuit or general sessions court, limited to the items the tenant disputed.

title: Statutory Dollar and Percentage Limits
bodyText: Tennessee sets few figures for residential leases. In the 17 Act counties a late fee may not exceed 10% of the rent past due and cannot be charged until a five-day grace period has run. Returned-payment charges are covered in the returned-payment rows. Contract interest is capped by the general interest statute. There is no cap on security deposits, application fees or pet fees, no statewide cap on rent increases, and no local government may control rent. A tenant who appeals a general sessions eviction judgment must post a bond, cash deposit, letter of credit or two sureties in the amount of one year's rent.

title: Late Fee Limits in Tennessee
bodyText: Tennessee limits late fees only in the 17 Act counties: no late charge until a five-day grace period has run (counting the due date, and carrying over to the next business day when the last day is a Sunday or legal holiday), and no charge, however labeled, above 10% of the rent past due. Outside the Act counties no statute sets a grace period or cap, though a court may refuse to enforce a fee it sees as a penalty. Tennessee has no separate late-fee cap for mobile home parks or subsidized housing.

title: Listing Fees in the Lease
bodyText: No Tennessee statute requires a lease to list every fee, to show rent and mandatory fees as one total, or to give notice before adding a fee. In the 17 Act counties every payment the lease requires is rent, and a rule adopted after the tenant signs binds the tenant only if reasonable notice is given and it does not substantially modify the lease, so a new fee should come by agreement or at renewal. Listing each fee in the lease is still good practice.

title: All-In Pricing and Fee Disclosure
bodyText: Tennessee has no all-in rent pricing law and no rule that mandatory fees appear on the lease's first page. Its fee-disclosure statute for hotel booking sites does not reach residential leases. The general Consumer Protection Act still bars unfair or deceptive acts, so advertised rent should not hide mandatory fees.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No Tennessee statute specifically bars charging a tenant a fee for a service the landlord does not provide. In the 17 Act counties fees the lease requires are rent and the landlord must perform the lease in good faith; charging for a service that is never delivered also risks a deceptive-practice claim under the Consumer Protection Act.

title: Pre-Set Deposit Charges
bodyText: No Tennessee statute allows or forbids a lease schedule of pre-set cleaning or repair charges against the deposit. In the 17 Act counties a deposit secures the landlord against damage beyond ordinary wear and tear and money damage from the tenant's breach, and damage found at the move-out inspection goes on the damage list with its estimated repair cost (damage found later is recoverable only within the statute's 30-day and 7-day limits), so a schedule is at most a guide to those estimates. Outside the Act counties the lease governs.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, if the tenant leaves owing nothing and a refund is due, the landlord sends notice of the refund amount to the tenant's last known address; if the tenant does not respond within 60 days, the landlord may keep the deposit free of the tenant's claim. Outside the Act counties no deposit statute applies, and an unclaimed refund the landlord owes may fall under Tennessee's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act, which presumes most property abandoned three years after the owner could first demand it and whose reporting rules apply to the holder. A lease clause forfeiting an unclaimed refund outside the Act counties should be avoided.

title: Paying a Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Tennessee gives tenants no right to pay a security deposit in installments; the landlord and tenant may agree to installments if they wish.

title: Last Month's Rent Deposits
bodyText: No Tennessee statute governs a deposit labeled as last month's rent or limits how a landlord applies one. In the 17 Act counties a security deposit secures damage and breach, and the landlord must return prepaid rent when the lease ends early under the Act's tenant remedies or a casualty; so money taken as last month's rent should be treated as prepaid rent, not as the security deposit.

title: Move-Out Notice and the Deposit
bodyText: Tennessee does not make the tenant's move-out notice a condition of getting the deposit back. In the 17 Act counties the notice matters to the inspection: when the landlord asks the tenant to vacate, or within five days after receiving the tenant's written notice of intent to vacate, the landlord may notify the tenant of the right to be present at the move-out inspection, and a tenant who leaves without giving written notice loses that inspection right.

title: Deposits After Abandonment
bodyText: Tennessee has no special fast procedure for the deposit of a tenant who abandons. In the 17 Act counties a tenant who abandoned or left without written notice has no right to the joint inspection, the landlord may apply the deposit to unpaid rent and other amounts, and an unanswered refund notice lets the landlord keep the deposit after 60 days. Outside the Act counties the lease governs.

title: Deposit Alternatives
bodyText: No Tennessee statute regulates a fee charged instead of a security deposit, such as a deposit-waiver or surety product. In the 17 Act counties a security deposit is money held to cover damage and breach, while a nonrefundable fee the lease requires is rent; a landlord offering an alternative should say plainly that the fee is not a deposit, is not refundable and does not limit the tenant's liability for damage, unless the product does.

title: Holding Deposits Before a Lease
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on holding deposits or other money taken before a lease is signed. Whether it is refundable depends on what the landlord and applicant agreed, so put the terms in writing: the amount, what it holds, how long, and whether it is credited to the deposit or rent or refunded if the landlord declines the applicant.

title: Notice of Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a separate written notice before a landlord may charge a nonrefundable fee. State plainly in the lease which payments are nonrefundable fees and which are the security deposit.

title: Where the Deposit Must Be Held
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a landlord who requires a deposit before occupancy must keep all tenants' deposits in an account used only for that purpose at a state- or federally-regulated bank or lending institution, and must tell the tenant at signing where the account is (not the account number). A landlord who neither used such an account nor gave the damage list may not keep any of the deposit. The Act requires no interest. Outside the Act counties no statute governs where a deposit is held.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the tenant cannot agree in the lease to give up the Act's deposit protections, because the Act bars any waiver of the tenant's rights or remedies under it. Outside the Act counties there are no statutory deposit rights to waive; the lease's own terms govern.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, unless otherwise agreed, a landlord who sells in a good-faith sale is released from liability under the lease and the Act for events after the tenant gets written notice of the sale and the deposit is transferred to the buyer. Outside the Act counties no statute addresses deposits on a sale; the lease and the sale contract govern who returns the deposit.

title: Consequences of Mishandling a Deposit
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a landlord may not keep any part of a deposit if the deposit was not kept in the required separate account and no damage list was provided as the Act requires. A tenant who disputes the final damage list may sue, but only over the items the tenant disputed. Tennessee sets no double or treble damages for deposit violations. Outside the Act counties no deposit statute applies.

title: Deposit Screening Standards
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule requiring a landlord to post or disclose the standards used to decide how much deposit an applicant pays. Applying different deposit amounts must still respect fair housing law.

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: No Tennessee landlord-tenant statute governs a utility deposit a landlord collects, or the return of a utility's own deposit to a tenant. A utility's own deposit is governed by the utility and its regulator, which this row does not cover. Unclaimed utility deposits and refunds are presumed abandoned one year after they become payable. In the county within the water-authority statute's population band (Hamilton County at the 2010 census), the water and wastewater authority may require a deposit of up to three months' average charges on the tenant's first bill.

title: Receiving Rent and the Duty to Maintain
bodyText: Tennessee did not adopt the uniform act's rule that forbids separating the right to receive rent from the duty to maintain the property. In the 17 Act counties the maintenance duties fall on the landlord by statute; a tenant may take on specified repairs only by a separate written agreement made in good faith, and the landlord may not make that agreement a condition of the lease.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Tennessee does not allow a landlord to lock out a tenant for unpaid rent. In the 17 Act counties the landlord may take possession only by court action, after abandonment or surrender, or as the Act permits, and not by cutting utilities or other essential services. In every county, entering and holding a home by force, threats or putting the occupant's goods out of doors is a forcible entry and detainer.

title: Can the Lease Waive Habitability?
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the landlord must comply with building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, and (in complexes of four or more units) provide garbage receptacles. A lease cannot remove those duties, because a tenant cannot waive the Act's rights. The landlord and tenant may agree in writing that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling, but only in good faith and not to evade the landlord's duties, and the landlord may not make that separate agreement a condition of the lease. Tennessee has no rule letting a tenant accept named defects for a rent reduction. Outside the Act counties no landlord-tenant statute sets a habitability duty, so the lease and local codes govern.

title: Changing Maintenance Duties by Agreement
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the only way to change who does maintenance is a separate written good-faith agreement for the tenant to do specified repairs or tasks, which the landlord may not make a condition of the lease. Nothing in the Act lets the lease drop a habitability duty, including for a home without a utility water supply. Essential services (utility services such as gas, heat and electricity, and other landlord obligations that materially affect health and safety) carry the Act's special remedies when the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply them, after the tenant's written notice. Outside the Act counties the lease governs.

title: Rights the Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a lease cannot make the tenant waive or give up any right or remedy under the Act, including the remedies for the landlord's noncompliance, failure to supply essential services, casualty, unlawful ouster and retaliation. A waiver term is unenforceable, and a landlord who willfully uses a lease containing terms known to be prohibited owes the tenant actual damages. The Act itself lets the lease change a few rules: the tenant may waive the notice of nonpayment (in 12-point bold type, without shortening the grace period); the landlord may show the unit in the last 30 days if the lease allows it and 24 hours' notice is given; the lease may set out the tenant's loss of the right to contest damages after missing a scheduled move-out inspection; the parties may agree separately that the tenant does specified repairs; and a few rules apply unless the parties agree otherwise. Outside the Act counties no general nonwaiver statute applies.

title: Waiving Eviction Notices
bodyText:
In the 17 Act counties the tenant may waive the notice of nonpayment of rent, so the landlord can file a detainer warrant as soon as the grace period ends; the waiver must be in the written lease in 12-point bold type or larger and cannot shorten the five-day grace period (the library's optional clause does this).

No other Act notice (the 14-day notices for breach, the 7-day notice for a repeat breach, or the notice to end a periodic tenancy) can be waived.

Outside the Act counties a general statute says no notice to quit is needed beyond service of the detainer warrant, but a later statute requires 14 days' notice for unpaid rent, damage, or violence or a real and present danger, 30 days for other defaults, and 3 days for violence, drug-related criminal activity or a threat to safety by a tenant who is not mentally or physically disabled or for an unauthorized occupant who refuses to leave (rental periods under 14 days excepted); whether a lease can waive those notices is unresolved, so do not rely on a waiver there.

title: Notice for Showings
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the landlord may enter to show the unit to prospective tenants during the final 30 days of the lease only if the lease grants that right and the tenant gets at least 24 hours' notice; a lease cannot shorten that notice. For other entries the Act sets no notice period: the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to show the unit to buyers, lenders or contractors, and the landlord may not abuse access or use it to harass. No separate signed document is required. Outside the Act counties no statute governs entry, so the lease governs; the library's 24-hour showing notice is the safe course in both tiers.

title: Smoke in Shared Areas
bodyText: Tennessee's Non-Smoker Protection Act bans smoking (including lighted hemp and vapor products) in lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums, trailer parks, retirement facilities and other multi-unit residential buildings, whether or not staff work there. Private residences are exempt, so state law does not ban smoking inside a unit, and no statute addresses smoke drifting between units or bars a lease from banning smoking in the unit. A lease cannot permit smoking in a common area. In the 17 Act counties a lease clause that makes the tenant give up complaints about smoke drift cannot waive the tenant's Act remedies.

title: Jury Waivers in Leases
bodyText: In Tennessee an eviction filed in general sessions court is tried by the judge without a jury in every county. A jury can decide a detainer case filed in circuit court. No Tennessee statute authorizes or bars a lease clause waiving a jury trial, and the statute of frauds does not require a separate signed writing for one. In the 17 Act counties a tenant cannot waive rights or remedies under the Act, but the jury right does not come from the Act. Because a pre-dispute jury waiver is a matter of case law and the state constitution, the library does not include one; take advice before adding one.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a lease may not have the tenant authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease; such a term is unenforceable. In every county a general statute declares void any power of attorney or authority to confess judgment given before a lawsuit is filed and served, and any judgment based on it. An older statute still allows a lease bond in which the tenant authorizes a confessed judgment for possession at the end of the term; the library offers it only as an optional clause outside the Act counties, and how it fits with the general voidness statute is unresolved, so take advice before relying on it.

title: Exculpatory and Indemnity Clauses
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a lease may not have the tenant agree to excuse or limit the landlord's liability to the tenant arising under law, or to indemnify the landlord for that liability or its costs; such a term is unenforceable, and a landlord who willfully uses one knowing it is prohibited owes the tenant actual damages. The Act itself requires the landlord to tell the tenant in writing that the landlord does not provide fire or casualty insurance for the tenant's belongings; that notice is not an exculpatory clause. Outside the Act counties no statute governs these clauses and their effect is a matter of case law; the library's clauses avoid exculpatory and indemnity language in every county.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, if a court finds a lease term was unconscionable when made, it enforces the rest of the lease without that term or limits the term to avoid an unconscionable result; the same applies to an unconscionable settlement of Act claims. Each side gets a chance to present evidence of the lease's setting, purpose and effect. By statute, a clause making it a default for the tenant to misrepresent a need for a service or support animal, or to give false animal documentation, is not unconscionable and is fully enforceable. Outside the Act counties no statute addresses unconscionable leases (the UCC rules cover goods), so case law governs. Tennessee has no rule letting a court rewrite a lease that later becomes excessively burdensome.

title: Accepting Rent After a Default
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, if the landlord accepts rent without reservation and knowing of a tenant's default, the landlord forgives that default and loses the right to terminate the lease for that breach. A landlord who wants to keep the right must refuse the payment or accept it with an express reservation at the time (in writing is safest). If the landlord does not sign a written lease, accepting rent without reservation binds the parties to a month-to-month tenancy. Outside the Act counties no statute decides whether accepting rent waives a default or a notice; case law was not searched, so the cautious course is the same: refuse or return rent for any period after a termination notice, or accept it only with a written reservation.

title: Penalty for Using Prohibited Terms
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a prohibited lease term is unenforceable, and a landlord who willfully provides a lease containing terms the landlord knows the Act prohibits is liable to the tenant for actual damages. The Act sets no fixed or multiple damages for this. From January 1, 2027, a separate rule protecting tenants' lawful firearm possession gives an adversely affected tenant its own remedies (declaratory and injunctive relief, actual and punitive damages and attorney fees). Outside the Act counties there is no such penalty.

title: Waiving Casualty and Mitigation Rules
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the tenant's right to leave and end the lease after a fire or other casualty that substantially impairs the unit (which the Act defines as the unit being deemed unfit for human habitation by a governmental authority), the return of prepaid rent and deposit, and the landlord's duty to mitigate cannot be waived by the tenant in the lease, because a tenant cannot waive the Act's rights or remedies. The landlord's own right to end the lease when restoration requires the tenant to leave is the landlord's to give up. Outside the Act counties an older statute lets a tenant who was not at fault surrender an untenantable building without owing later rent, and a covenant to keep the premises in repair does not make the tenant rebuild after a casualty that was not the tenant's fault; both rules give way to an express written agreement to the contrary. No non-Act statute sets a duty to mitigate.

title: Homestead and Exemption Waivers
bodyText: Tennessee's homestead exemption protects real property an individual owns and uses as a principal residence. It may be given up only in an instrument that conveys the property, never in a note or other instrument that does not convey property, and a married person's homestead only with both spouses' consent; so a lease should not contain a homestead waiver. A Tennessee resident also has a $10,000 personal property exemption from execution, claimed by filing a sworn list with the court (a list filed after the judgment becomes final does not reach an execution already issued), plus absolute exemptions for necessary clothing, family portraits and pictures, and the family Bible and school books. No statute lets a lease waive these exemptions, and the library's lease contains no exemption waiver.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Leases
bodyText: Tennessee's Uniform Arbitration Act (in force since July 1, 2023, for agreements whenever made) makes a written agreement to arbitrate existing or future disputes valid and enforceable, except on grounds that would revoke any contract. Before a dispute arises a party cannot waive certain protections, including the right to be represented by a lawyer. No section found in a whole-Code search adds a special rule for leases or homes, excludes claims by type, or keeps possession cases in court. In the 17 Act counties the Act's rights are enforceable by legal action and cannot be waived, so whether an arbitration clause can reach Act remedies or an eviction is unsettled. The library does not include an arbitration clause.

title: Abandonment, Remaining Rent and Mitigation
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the lease stays enforceable for rent for the rest of the term even after the landlord gives notice of a breach or files a detainer warrant, but the injured party must mitigate damages. If the tenant abandons, the landlord must make reasonable efforts to rerent at a fair rental; a new tenancy that starts before the old term ends terminates the old lease from that date (for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy the term counts as one month or one week). Abandonment is shown prima facie by 30 days' unexplained absence without paying rent, or by 15 days' nonpayment plus signs of moving out (then only after a posted and mailed 10-day notice). Outside the Act counties no statute sets a duty to rerent or mitigate.

title: Tenant Remedies for the Landlord's Breach
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, after giving the landlord 14 days' written notice, a tenant may recover damages, get an injunction and recover reasonable attorney's fees for the landlord's noncompliance with the lease or the Act. If the lease ends for noncompliance after sufficient notice, the landlord must return prepaid rent and the recoverable deposit. Separate remedies cover failure to supply essential services, fire or casualty, unlawful ouster or cutting off services, abusive entry and retaliation. The Act does not spell out a tenant's own right to terminate for ordinary noncompliance. Outside the Act counties no statute sets tenant remedies; the lease and general contract law govern.

title: Landlord's Remedies After Termination
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, when the lease is terminated the landlord may claim possession and rent, and separately actual damages for the breach and reasonable attorney's fees; the lease also stays enforceable for rent for the rest of the term, subject to the duty to mitigate. The landlord may also recover damages and an injunction for the tenant's noncompliance, punitive damages for willful destruction, and the cost of curing the tenant's maintenance breach as rent. The landlord may not take possession except by court action, abandonment or surrender. In every county a detainer case is tried in general sessions court by the judge, who decides possession and the rent arrearage, interest and damages, or in circuit court with a jury.

title: Tenant Remedies for Failure to Repair
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a tenant whose landlord fails to repair may, after 14 days' written notice, sue for damages, an injunction and attorney's fees. If the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply essential services (such as gas, heat or electricity), the tenant who gives written notice may buy the services and deduct the actual, reasonable cost from rent, recover the lost rental value, or move to substitute housing and pay no rent meanwhile. Tennessee has no general repair-and-deduct remedy for other repairs and no rent escrow or rent deposit with a court clerk. Outside the Act counties no statute gives a repair remedy.

title: Repair Requests in Writing
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the tenant's statutory repair remedies already turn on written notice: 14 days' written notice for damages and an injunction, and written notice before the essential-services remedies. A lease may ask for repair requests in writing or through a portal, but it cannot take away the Act's remedies, and a lease that lets the tenant give notice another way simply gives the tenant more. When the tenant must make repairs to cure the tenant's own breach, the tenant must ask in writing and the landlord must authorize them in writing first. Outside the Act counties no statute governs repair notices.

title: Ending a Lease When Repairs Are Too Costly
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule letting a landlord end a lease because repairs would cost too much. In the 17 Act counties the landlord may end the lease on 14 days' written notice only if fire or casualty damage means restoring the unit requires the tenant to move out, and a landlord whose code compliance requires alteration or demolition that would deprive the tenant of the unit may bring a possession action despite the retaliation rule. Outside the Act counties the lease governs.

title: Rent Into Court and Counterclaims
bodyText: Tennessee does not require a tenant to pay rent into court to raise a defense in a general sessions eviction, and no statute makes a tenant's counterclaim mandatory. To appeal a general sessions possession judgment, the tenant must post a bond, cash deposit, letter of credit or two sureties in the amount of one year's rent; if the tenant does not, the landlord needs no bond to get possession.

title: When a Tenant May End a Lease Early by Law
Cure Periods and Eviction Grounds
bodyText:
In the 17 Act counties, for a material breach or a tenant-duty breach that materially affects health and safety, the landlord's written notice may give 14 days to cure a breach curable by paying rent, repairs, damages or another amount owed, or end the lease in at least 14 days if the breach cannot be cured; a substantially similar breach within six months allows termination on 7 days' notice. Violence, a real and present danger, a hazardous or unsanitary condition, or an unauthorized occupant refusing to leave allows termination 3 days after the tenant receives notice.

Outside the Act counties the notice is 14 days for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear (both with a right to cure) or violence or a real and present danger; 30 days for other defaults; and 3 days for violence, drug-related criminal activity or danger by a tenant who is not mentally or physically disabled, or for an unauthorized occupant who refuses to leave. Those notice rules do not apply to rental periods of less than 14 days.

In the Act counties the lease may give more time but not less, except the nonpayment-notice waiver the Act allows; outside them, whether a lease can shorten these notices is unresolved. Whether a breach is material is for the court, except that the Act makes a misrepresented need for a service or support animal a material noncompliance.

title: Rent After Condemnation
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute barring a landlord from collecting rent after a unit is condemned or ordered vacated. In the 17 Act counties a tenant may stop paying rent while living in substitute housing when the landlord fails to supply essential services, may terminate after a casualty that substantially impairs the unit (deemed unfit for human habitation by a governmental authority), and may recover damages for the landlord's failure to keep the unit fit and habitable. A court may also declare an unfit building a public nuisance and appoint a receiver (see the receivership row), and local ordinances may add their own rules.

title: Demand for Rent Before Eviction
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties rent is payable without demand at the agreed time and place, so the landlord need not demand rent before giving the notice of nonpayment. Outside the Act counties the 14-day termination notice for unpaid rent applies to rent that is due and in arrears upon demand, so a landlord there should demand the rent (in writing is safest) before or with the notice.

title: Landlord's Promises to Repair
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule that a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit must be in writing, carry a completion date or be made before the lease is signed. A promise made to induce a tenant to rent can still support a deceptive-practice claim under the Consumer Protection Act if it is false, so put any promised work and its date in the lease.

title: Who Does the Repairs
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute letting a landlord name the repairer a tenant must use, or requiring licensed contractors for tenant repairs. Because the Act has no general repair-and-deduct remedy, the question mostly does not arise. When a tenant makes repairs to cure the tenant's own breach in an Act county, the tenant must request them in writing and the landlord must authorize them in writing first.

title: Shifting Maintenance to the Tenant
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the landlord and tenant may agree in writing that the tenant will do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling, but only in good faith and not to evade the landlord's duties, and the landlord may not make that separate agreement a condition of the lease. The statute requires no particular consideration, but the work must be specified; a general clause putting all maintenance on the tenant does not meet it. Outside the Act counties the lease governs; the library's tenant-repair agreement is written to work in both tiers.

title: Tenant's Duties Under Tennessee Law
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the tenant must comply with building and housing code duties that fall on tenants and materially affect health and safety; keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as clean and safe as when the tenant moved in; put garbage and waste in the designated receptacles; not damage the premises or allow others to, and not engage in illegal conduct there; and make sure the tenant and guests do not disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. The tenant must also follow reasonable rules the tenant had notice of, not unreasonably refuse entry, use the unit only as a dwelling unless otherwise agreed, and give notice of an absence over seven days if the lease requires it. Outside the Act counties these duties come from the lease.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on renting the same unit or room to two tenants at once. A tenant who is kept out because the landlord rented to someone else has the Act's remedies for the landlord's noncompliance and unlawful exclusion in the 17 Act counties, and contract remedies elsewhere.

title: Keeping a Victim-Tenant's Information Private
