bodyText: In every Tennessee county, when a tenant ends a lease early as a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking, the landlord may not reveal any information that could reasonably be used to locate the former tenant or household member (such as a home or work address, telephone number or social security number) without the tenant's written consent, unless law or a court requires it. Separately, the Secretary of State's address confidentiality program gives certified victims a substitute address; government entities must accept it, and a participant may ask a landlord or other private business to use it, though the statute does not require a private business to agree.

title: Deposits After a Victim's Early Termination
bodyText: Tennessee has no special deposit timetable when a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking ends a lease early. The terminating tenant still owes rent for the full month in which the tenancy ends and earlier obligations, and other parties to the lease are not released. In the 17 Act counties the ordinary deposit rules apply (inspection, damage list and refund notice); the Act's deposit steps run as usual and set no special timing for a household where some occupants stay. Outside the Act counties the lease governs the deposit.

title: Eviction Protection for Victims
bodyText: In every Tennessee county, if domestic abuse is the reason a tenancy is being ended, only the perpetrator may be evicted; the victims, children under 18 and innocent occupants may not be evicted solely because of the abuse. The protection applies only after the victim obtains an order of protection for that incident (ordering the perpetrator out or away from the home, or finding a danger) and gives the landlord a copy, and it ends if the order is dismissed or the victim and adult tenants break their written agreement to keep the perpetrator away. Separately, the early-termination statutes say they do not authorize evicting a tenant solely because the tenant or a household member is a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking. A victim can still be evicted for nonpayment or another lease violation.

title: Lock Changes for Victims
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute giving a domestic-violence victim a right to have the locks changed or to change them, and none voids a lease term on the subject. An order of protection may give the victim possession of the home and evict the abuser, and in every county a landlord who receives such an order can remove the perpetrator from the lease. Changing locks promptly when a victim-tenant asks, with the cost handled as the lease provides, is the cautious course.

title: Where Tennessee's Protection-Order Law Is
bodyText: Tennessee's orders of protection are in Title 36, Chapter 3, Part 6 of the Code. The definitions of domestic abuse, sexual assault and stalking victims that the landlord-tenant statutes borrow are in § 36-3-601; the petition is § 36-3-602; ex parte orders, the hearing within 15 days and extensions for up to one year at a time (up to five years after a violation, ten after a second) are § 36-3-605; and what an order may include (such as giving the victim the home) is § 36-3-606. The tenant protections themselves are in § 66-7-109(e) and § 66-7-112 for every county and § 66-28-205 and § 66-28-517(g) in the Act counties. 2025 Pub. Ch. 62 amended Part 6; the sections relied on here were read in their current form.

title: Documents a Victim-Tenant Must Give
bodyText: Tennessee's two victim protections use different documents. To end a lease early, the tenant gives written notice requesting release, a mutually agreed release date within 30 days, and either a valid order of protection issued or extended after a hearing that found the tenant or household member a victim, or documentation of a criminal charge of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking based on a police report; the document must be dated no more than 60 days before the tenant's notice. For the rule that only the perpetrator may be evicted, the victim must have an order of protection for the specific incident, with one of the listed terms (perpetrator out, away from the home, or a danger finding), and give the landlord a copy; no time limit applies, but the protection ends if the order is dismissed. There is no lock-change document list because there is no lock-change statute.

title: Lawn Care and Irrigation
bodyText: In Tennessee the lease itself should not make the tenant responsible for lawn care or irrigation. In the 17 Act counties a tenant may take on specified maintenance tasks such as mowing, leaf raking or following an irrigation schedule only by a separate written agreement made in good faith, which the landlord may not make a condition of the lease; the library's tenant-repair agreement is that document and is used in every county. No Tennessee statute makes tenants keep trees or plants clear of power lines.

title: Snow and Ice Removal
bodyText: No Tennessee statute assigns snow and ice removal between landlord and tenant. In the 17 Act counties the landlord must keep common areas clean and safe, and a tenant may take on snow removal for the areas the tenant uses only by the separate written good-faith agreement the Act allows; the library's tenant-repair agreement covers it. Some city charters let the city remove snow and ice from sidewalks and charge the cost to the abutting property, which falls on the owner.

title: Key Control
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a key-control policy, background checks for employees with key access, or rekeying between tenants. The library's Keys clause covers issuing and returning keys and the cost of rekeying when the tenant loses them.

title: Homeowners' Associations and Renting
bodyText: If a homeowners' association amends its declaration to ban or effectively ban long-term rentals (180 days or more) of single-family houses, an owner who owned the house before the amendment keeps a vested right to rent it as a long-term rental until the owner transfers it. Tennessee has no statute capping an association's lease-approval fees, letting an association collect rent directly from a tenant when the owner is delinquent, or limiting what tenant information an association may require. A tenant must follow the association rules the lease makes binding, and fines the owner passes on are lease charges.

title: Telling Tenants About Association Rules
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a lease of a condominium or homeowners'-association home to disclose the association's obligations or documents to the tenant, or requiring a statement about the condominium law in the lease. Because a tenant can follow only rules the tenant knows about, give the tenant a copy of the association rules with the lease.

title: Tampering With Smoke Alarms
bodyText: Tennessee makes it unlawful for anyone to tamper with or remove a required smoke alarm, or a component of one, in a one- or two-family rental unit, and owners of apartment buildings and one- or two-family rentals must install approved smoke alarms. No statute sets or caps a lease fee for tampering. The lease may make the tenant pay the actual cost of repairing or replacing an alarm the tenant damaged.

title: Pool Safety at Rentals
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a residential landlord to fence a pool or give a pool-safety notice. The state's public swimming pool permit law covers public swimming pools as it defines them and does not apply to privately owned swimming facilities built on private property by a group of not more than 20 households; local codes may add rules. In the 17 Act counties the general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-304(a)).

title: Window Guards
bodyText: Tennessee has no window-guard statute and no required window-guard lease notice. In the 17 Act counties the general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-304(a)).

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute setting a maximum water-heater temperature for a rental before a new tenant moves in. In the 17 Act counties the general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-304(a)).

title: Radiator Covers
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on steam radiator covers or a related lease rider. In the 17 Act counties the general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-304(a)).

title: Waterbeds
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on waterbeds in rentals. A lease may restrict them or require insurance.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators
bodyText: Tennessee does not require a landlord to supply a stove or refrigerator. If the lease includes appliances, the library's appliance clauses say who maintains them. In the 17 Act counties the general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-304(a)).

title: Appliances Not Included
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule presuming that appliances in a unit are supplied by the landlord unless the lease excludes them. List the appliances the landlord supplies and any the lease excludes. In the 17 Act counties essential services the landlord supplies (such as heat) are governed by the Act regardless of the list.

title: Balcony Inspections
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks or other exterior elevated elements of rental buildings. In the 17 Act counties the general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-304(a)).

title: Fire Sprinklers
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a residential landlord to retrofit fire sprinklers. The state fire marshal's building construction safety standards, adopted by rule, set requirements for new and existing buildings by occupancy; local codes may add more.

title: Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a residential lease to disclose whether the building has fire sprinklers, and no grant or loan program for private sprinkler retrofits was found in the Code.

title: Asbestos
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a residential landlord to notify tenants about asbestos. Its asbestos statutes concern asbestos lawsuits and trusts, school buildings and contractor licensing; federal work-practice rules may apply to renovation.

title: Private Well Testing
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to test a private well or give test results to tenants. In the 17 Act counties the general duties still apply: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-304(a)).

title: Lead-Safe Certificates
bodyText: Tennessee has no lead-safe certificate that must be attached to a lease. Its lead statute certifies lead-abatement professionals and makes it unlawful to perform abatement without certification; the federal lead disclosure still applies to pre-1978 housing.

title: State Lead Notices
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing, Tennessee requires no state lead notice, certificate or packet for tenants. State law regulates who may perform lead abatement.

title: Defective Drywall
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring disclosure of defective (for example, imported corrosive) drywall to tenants.

title: Toxic Chemical Warnings
bodyText: Tennessee has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65 warning requirement for rental housing.

title: Environmental Contamination
bodyText: No Tennessee statute requires a residential lease to disclose environmental contamination or to incorporate recorded environmental use limitations. The residential property disclosure law applies to sales, not leases; methamphetamine quarantine rules are covered separately.

title: Military and Airport Zones
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a lease to disclose military air installation noise or accident zones, and no related termination right.

title: Shoreline Access
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a lease to disclose shoreline or public-access rights.

title: Ordnance and Demolition Notices
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a lease to disclose former ordnance locations or planned demolition.

title: Bed Bug Cooperation
bodyText: Tennessee has no bed bug statute requiring tenant cooperation or landlord treatment. In the 17 Act counties the tenant must keep the premises clean and safe and not unreasonably refuse entry for necessary services, and the landlord must keep the premises fit and habitable.

title: Pest Control Notices
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to give tenants advance notice of pesticide application or pest-control service. In the 17 Act counties the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to supply necessary or agreed services.

title: Locks and Security Devices
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring deadbolts, door viewers or other security devices in rentals, or rekeying between tenants.

title: Smart Locks and App Entry
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute regulating smart locks or app-based entry systems in rentals. Entry limits still apply: in the 17 Act counties a landlord may not abuse access or use it to harass the tenant.

title: Window and Portable Air Conditioners
bodyText: Tennessee gives tenants no right to install a portable or window air conditioner, and no statute limits a lease that restricts them. A lease may require approval and safe installation.

title: Plug-In Solar Devices
bodyText: Tennessee gives tenants no right to install a plug-in or balcony solar device. Its solar statutes concern solar-facility land agreements and utility-scale projects.

title: Recycling Notices
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to tell tenants how to recycle. In the 17 Act counties complexes of four or more units must provide receptacles for garbage and waste, and tenants must use them.

title: Where Tennessee's Building and Fire Codes Are
bodyText: Tennessee's minimum statewide building construction safety standards are adopted by the state fire marshal by rule under Tenn. Code Ann. § 68-120-101 and may be drawn from national codes such as those of the International Code Council and the National Fire Protection Association; local governments may adopt codes by reference. The section was amended by 2025 Pub. Ch. 149 and 2026 Pub. Ch. 958, but the construction code has not moved to a new title.

title: Codes Adopted by Edition
bodyText: No Tennessee landlord-tenant statute incorporates a building or housing code frozen at a particular edition. In the 17 Act counties the landlord must comply with the applicable building and housing codes as they stand; the statewide standards are set by fire-marshal rule and local codes by local adoption.

title: Heat
bodyText: Tennessee sets no minimum indoor temperature for rentals. In the 17 Act counties heat is an essential service: if the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply it, the tenant may, after written notice, buy heat and deduct the cost, recover the lost rental value, or move to substitute housing and pay no rent meanwhile. Who pays for heat follows the lease; the Act has no rule limiting a shift to the tenant beyond the essential-services remedy.

title: Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: Tennessee does not require a lease to disclose a certificate of occupancy. In a city that creates a rental inspection district, residential rental units in the district are subject to inspection, and a property that passes and stays in compliance can be exempted.

title: Elevators and Other Building Equipment
bodyText: Tennessee has a separate elevator-safety chapter that covers elevators, dumbwaiters and escalators; no consumer-protection or product-safety statute puts a separate duty on a landlord for other building facilities such as garage doors.

title: Sex Offender Residence Limits
bodyText: Tennessee's residence limits fall on the offender, not the landlord: a registered sexual offender or violent sexual offender may not knowingly establish a residence within 1,000 feet of a school, licensed day care center, other child care facility, public park, playground, recreation center or public athletic field, or within 1,000 feet of a former victim. No statute makes a landlord check distances, disclose offenders or refuse an applicant; fair housing and screening rules still apply.

title: Submetering and Separate Utility Billing
bodyText: Tennessee has no landlord-tenant statute governing submetering or a landlord's separate billing of utilities, and no required disclosure for it. State the method, the rate and any fee in the lease. In the county within the water-authority statute's population band (Hamilton County at the 2010 census), that statute applies only where the unit is not submetered or billed by allocation.

title: Reselling Electricity to Tenants
bodyText: No Tennessee statute found says whether a landlord who resells electricity or gas to tenants by meter becomes a regulated utility, or requires a disclosure for it. Before reselling energy, check with the Tennessee Public Utility Commission and the local utility.

title: Splitting Unmetered Utilities
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute making a lease term unenforceable because it makes the tenant pay for utilities not separately metered to the unit, and none sets an allocation formula. In the 17 Act counties utility charges the lease requires are rent; state the formula in the lease.

title: Master-Metered Electricity
bodyText: No Tennessee statute found bars passing master-metered electricity to tenants or requires a fixed allowance. Federally subsidized housing has its own utility-allowance rules.

title: Utility Disclosures
bodyText: Tennessee requires no utility-cost disclosure attached to the lease. The library's utilities clause says which utilities the landlord provides and which the tenant must put in the tenant's name.

title: Utilities Left in the Landlord's Name
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, if a written lease requires the tenant to put utility service in the tenant's name and the tenant does not do so within three days after occupancy, the landlord may have the service terminated if it is in the landlord's name. Otherwise the landlord may not interrupt essential services, and doing so willfully is unlawful ouster with damages and fees. Outside the Act counties no statute governs; do not cut services as a way to remove a tenant.

title: Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: Tennessee has no general statute adding winter time to a utility's disconnection notice for tenants. The state fire marshal or its inspectors may disconnect a residential customer's electricity only after finding an immediate danger, trying to reach the customer or owner, and checking for electric medical devices. Utility disconnection rules otherwise come from the utility and its regulator.

title: Notice of a Tenant's Pending Shutoff
bodyText: No Tennessee statute lets or requires a utility to notify the owner of a tenant's pending disconnection. Ask the utility whether it offers landlord notification by agreement.

title: Interruptions of Landlord-Supplied Utilities
bodyText: Tennessee has no separate rule for interruptions of electricity a landlord supplies through a submeter. In the 17 Act counties a landlord who willfully interrupts essential services is liable for unlawful ouster, and a tenant has the essential-services remedies.

title: Tenants' Unpaid Water and Sewer Bills
bodyText: Tennessee has no general statute letting a lease clause and an affidavit keep a tenant's unpaid water or sewer bill from becoming a lien on the property. In the county within the water-authority statute's population band (Hamilton County at the 2010 census), the water-authority acknowledgment form, sent within one business day, stops the authority from collecting the tenant's delinquent charges from the owner. Elsewhere, local utility rules govern.

title: Energy-Efficiency Meter Charges
bodyText: Tennessee has no meter conservation charge requiring landlord notice to new tenants or a rent deduction.

title: Tenants' Energy Usage Data
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on releasing a tenant's energy usage data to the owner for benchmarking, and none requiring a lease authorization for it. Utilities set their own data-release rules; a lease clause authorizing release is a matter of consent.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Areas
bodyText: Tennessee gives tenants no right to install an EV charger. From 2026, a homeowners' association (as that part of the Code defines it) may not prohibit a property owner from installing a charger for personal use on the owner's property or designated parking space; that protects owners, not tenants. No statute governs chargers in a landlord's shared parking areas.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on removing, leaving or paying for a tenant-installed EV charger at the end of a tenancy. Put any agreed installation, ownership and removal terms in writing.

title: Charging Tenants for EV Power
bodyText: No Tennessee statute found puts a landlord who charges tenants for EV charging under weights-and-measures or utility regulation. Check with the Public Utility Commission and the local utility before reselling power.

title: Cable and Internet Access
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute giving cable or satellite providers access to multifamily buildings or limiting exclusive arrangements. Federal rules on over-the-air antennas may apply.

title: Recording Long Leases
bodyText: A Tennessee lease for more than three years must be in writing, and to be valid against anyone other than the landlord, the landlord's heirs and devisees, and persons with actual notice, it must be proved and registered with the county register. Shorter leases need not be recorded.

title: Leases That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Tennessee no action may be brought on a lease of land for longer than one year unless the lease, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged. A lease for more than three years must also be written and registered to bind third parties.

title: Formalities for Longer Leases
bodyText: Tennessee requires no seal or special execution formality for a residential lease. A lease longer than one year must be in a signed writing to be enforced, and one longer than three years must be in writing and registered to bind third parties.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to give the tenant a signed copy of the lease, and failure to do so is not a defense. In the 17 Act counties the landlord must disclose in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, who manages the premises and who receives notices, and must tell the tenant at signing where the deposit account is. Giving a signed copy is the safe practice.

title: Required Lease Contents
bodyText: Tennessee has no list of required lease contents and no rule that the start and end dates appear on the first page. In the 17 Act counties the landlord must give a written statement that the landlord does not provide insurance for the tenant's belongings and the deposit-account location; the nonpayment-notice waiver, if used, must be in 12-point bold; and the move-out inspection waiver must be set out in the lease.

title: Type Size in Leases
bodyText: Tennessee sets no minimum type size for a whole residential lease. The one size rule is in the Act counties: a tenant's waiver of the nonpayment notice must be in 12-point bold type or larger.

title: Initialing Lease Provisions
bodyText: No Tennessee statute requires a tenant to initial particular lease provisions. Initialing important optional clauses is still good evidence that the tenant saw them.

title: Month-to-Month Versus Fixed-Term Terms
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute barring lease terms that are more burdensome for month-to-month tenants than for fixed-term tenants, or the reverse.

title: Plain Language and Consumer Statements
bodyText: Tennessee has no plain-language statute for residential leases and no required statement of consumer rights in the lease.

title: Translated Leases
bodyText: Tennessee prescribes no verbatim lease text and no duty to translate a lease into the language in which it was negotiated.

title: Truth in Renting
bodyText: Tennessee has no truth-in-renting act requiring a state statement of tenant rights or barring lease terms that violate clearly established rights. In the 17 Act counties prohibited terms are unenforceable, and a landlord who willfully uses known prohibited terms owes actual damages.

title: State Rights Guides
bodyText: Tennessee has no state-published landlord-tenant rights guide that a landlord must give before signing or at renewal.

title: Tenant Rights Statements
bodyText: Tennessee has no state-agency statement of tenant rights that a landlord must provide with a signed acknowledgment, and no rule barring suit until one is given.

title: Notice of Tenant-Protection Coverage
bodyText: Tennessee has no just-cause or rent-increase law, so no lease must say whether a unit is covered by one. Required disclosures in Tennessee are few: in the Act counties, the manager and notice addresses, the deposit account location and the landlord's insurance statement; statewide, the federal lead disclosure for older housing.

title: Automatic Lease Renewal
bodyText: Tennessee's automatic-renewal statute governs subscription and continuous-service offers charged to a consumer's card or account (clear terms, affirmative consent, an acknowledgment and an easy cancellation method); it does not mention leases of real property, and whether it reaches a lease that renews automatically is untested. No landlord-tenant statute limits automatic renewal; a renewing lease should state the renewal term and how either party can stop it.

title: Guarantors and Renewals
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute limiting a lease guarantor's liability to the original term. Whether a guaranty covers renewals depends on its words, so the guaranty should say expressly whether it covers renewals and extensions.

title: Changing Terms of a Month-to-Month Lease
bodyText: Tennessee has no specific notice period for changing the terms of a month-to-month tenancy. In the 17 Act counties a month-to-month tenancy can be ended on 30 days' written notice before a rental date, and a landlord rule adopted mid-tenancy binds only with reasonable notice and if it does not substantially modify the lease; the safe course is to give at least 30 days' written notice before a change takes effect at the start of a rental period.

title: Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a party has notice of a fact if the party actually knows it or has been given written notice, and all parties must give written notice to the last known or designated address in the lease; the Act's termination, cure, repair and deposit notices are written. If the tenant gives an email address in the lease, the landlord may send notices by email unless a section requires another form, but the landlord may not require an email address. Outside the Act counties the § 66-7-109 notices and the lease govern.

title: Extra Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a party has notice of a fact if the party actually knows it or was given written notice to the address in the lease, and email may be used if the tenant gave an email address in the lease. The Act does not bar the parties from agreeing on an additional delivery method such as text message, but where a section requires written notice, a text should be in addition to, not instead of, written delivery.

title: Tenancy at Will
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute defining a tenancy at will or setting its notice. In the 17 Act counties, if the landlord does not sign a written lease, accepting rent without reservation creates a month-to-month tenancy, ended on 30 days' written notice; people who take possession without paying rent or signing are trespassers unless the landlord accepts rent from them.

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Tennessee's landlord-tenant act excludes transient occupancy in a hotel or motel, and Tennessee treats short-term rentals mainly through tax and local land-use law; a separate part of Title 13 addresses local rules that prohibit short-term rental units. There is no separate seasonal-tenancy statute; a seasonal lease of a dwelling is otherwise an ordinary tenancy.

title: Leases With an Option to Purchase
bodyText: Tennessee's residential property disclosure law applies to a lease with an option to buy residential property of one to four units, so a landlord who grants a purchase option must give the owner's disclosure (or the permitted disclaimer) as for a sale. No landlord-tenant statute otherwise regulates option clauses.

title: Reasonable Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Under the Tennessee Human Rights Act a landlord may not refuse reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when needed to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling, or refuse reasonable modifications at the disabled person's expense (for a rental, the landlord may condition a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior, reasonable wear and tear excepted). Physically disabled and blind persons are also entitled to full and equal access to rental housing, and in buildings of three or more stories they get priority for units on the first two floors. Federal fair housing law applies too.

title: Questions About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: Tennessee law makes it a discriminatory practice to use a rental application form, or make a record of inquiry in connection with a prospective rental, that indicates a limitation, specification or discrimination based on race, color, creed, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. Keep application questions to what is needed to screen, and do not record protected characteristics.

title: Children and Occupancy
bodyText: Tennessee does not require a lease to address occupancy by children. Familial status is protected under the Tennessee Human Rights Act, so a landlord may not refuse to rent or set different terms because of children, except in qualifying housing for older persons; reasonable occupancy limits set by law still apply.

title: Penalty for Refusing a Guide Dog
bodyText: In Tennessee a legally blind person with a guide dog from a recognized training school may not be denied the right to lease a dwelling because of the dog, may not be charged a deposit for it, and may not be restricted as to where the dog goes while with its owner. A landlord who refuses to lease for that reason, or otherwise violates the rule, commits a Class C misdemeanor. Other disability-related denials are civil fair housing violations.

title: Misrepresenting a Service or Support Animal
bodyText: Yes, Tennessee's penalty reaches housing: knowingly misrepresenting a disability or disability-related need as part of a request to keep a service or support animal in residential rental property, or giving a landlord documentation that falsely says an animal is a service or support animal, is a Class B misdemeanor (with 100 hours of community service for misrepresenting a service animal). The landlord may also treat it as a material default under the lease.

title: Caring for Animals Left Behind
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute giving a landlord a right to enter to care for a tenant's animal or setting what to do with animals left behind. In the 17 Act counties the landlord may enter at reasonable times during a tenant's absence of more than seven days and after abandonment; in an emergency the landlord may enter without consent.

title: Pet and Eviction Fact Sheets
bodyText: Tennessee has no state fact sheet on pets and eviction that a landlord must give with the lease.

title: Cannabis
bodyText: Tennessee has no medical or adult-use cannabis program that protects tenants, and no statute limits a lease ban on cannabis. Smoking lighted hemp or vaping hemp-derived cannabinoids counts as smoking under the Non-Smoker Protection Act, and the library's smoking clause bans smoking on the property.

title: Drug-Free Housing Addenda
bodyText: Tennessee prescribes no drug-free housing addendum. A tenancy may be terminated where the premises or the area immediately around them is knowingly used for listed drug or prostitution offenses, and in the 17 Act counties violence or a real danger allows a 3-day termination.

title: Fast Termination for Criminal Activity
bodyText: Tennessee has no separate expedited court track for criminal-activity evictions. In the 17 Act counties a landlord may terminate on 3 days' written notice for violence, a real and present danger, a hazardous condition or an unauthorized occupant who refuses to leave; outside them 3 days' notice suffices for violence, drug-related criminal activity or danger by a tenant who is not mentally or physically disabled. A tenancy may also be terminated for knowing drug or prostitution use of the premises. The detainer case then follows the ordinary procedure.

title: Hardship Stays of Eviction
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute letting a court delay an eviction for hardship. A writ of possession from general sessions court generally may not issue until 10 days after judgment, and a tenant who appeals must post the bond of one year's rent.

title: Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on naming minors as eviction defendants. Detainer summons may be served on any adult found in possession.

title: Who May Appear for an Entity Landlord
bodyText: No Tennessee statute found decides whether a non-attorney may appear in court for a corporate or LLC landlord. That question is governed by court rules and the law on unauthorized practice; take advice or use a lawyer.

title: Tenant Bankruptcy
bodyText: Tennessee law does not address eviction after a tenant files bankruptcy; the federal automatic stay and its exceptions govern.

title: Delayed Benefit or Voucher Payments
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule requiring a continuance or reinstatement when a tenant's government benefit or voucher payment is late.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Tennessee gives tenants no statutory right to stop an eviction by paying the rent owed after the case is filed. In the 17 Act counties a tenant may cure a rent default within the 14-day notice period (unless the notice was waived), and a landlord who accepts rent without reservation knowing of the default waives termination for that breach; partial payments should be accepted only with a written reservation.

title: Relief From Lease Forfeiture
bodyText: No Tennessee statute gives a tenant relief from forfeiture of a residential lease after default.

title: Barring Trespassers
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a person who takes possession without paying rent and without signing the landlord's lease, or who enters without an oral agreement, is a trespasser who may be evicted at once and held liable for damages and rent; if the landlord accepts rent from them, they become tenants. In every county an owner may use the limited sheriff procedure to remove unauthorized persons who were never tenants. Barring a non-tenant from common areas relies on the general criminal trespass law (Tenn. Code Ann. § 39-14-405, not reviewed here).

title: Guests and Visitors
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute giving tenants' guests or service providers a right of access in multi-unit buildings or barring guest fees. The lease's guest rules govern, subject to fair housing law.

title: Good-Cause Notices
bodyText: Tennessee has no good-cause eviction rule, so no notice must state good cause for ending a tenancy.

title: Owner Move-In
bodyText: Tennessee has no owner-move-in rule; with no good-cause requirement, a landlord may end a periodic tenancy with the required notice or decline to renew a fixed term without stating a reason. An early-termination right for owner occupancy exists only if the lease grants it.

title: Cold-Weather Eviction Limits
bodyText: Tennessee has no cold-weather limit or extra notice before a tenant must vacate.

title: Alterations During a Notice to Vacate
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule forbidding alterations that make a unit uninhabitable while a notice to vacate is pending. In the 17 Act counties the landlord's habitability and essential-services duties continue until the tenancy ends, and willfully interrupting services is unlawful ouster.

title: Alternate Housing
bodyText: Tennessee imposes no general duty on a landlord to relocate a tenant. In the 17 Act counties, if the landlord fails to supply essential services, the tenant may choose to procure reasonable substitute housing and is excused from rent meanwhile, and may recover its reasonable value and attorney's fees; the remedy is the tenant's choice after written notice.

title: Rent Paid in Installments
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties, unless otherwise agreed, periodic rent for a term of one month or less is payable at the start of the term and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the start of each month, and rent may be apportioned day by day if the parties agree. A lease may set its own schedule. Outside the Act counties the lease governs.

title: Rent Escalation Clauses
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on rent escalation clauses and no retaliation safe harbor that depends on one. A fixed-term lease may include an escalation clause if its terms are stated; in the 17 Act counties a rent increase to retaliate for a deposit complaint or use of Act remedies is barred.

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText: No Tennessee statute governs a residential lease clause passing real estate tax increases to the tenant. A lease may include one if it states the method and the tenant's share; in the Act counties the charge is rent.

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on rent concessions (free months or move-in discounts). State the concession and any condition for keeping it in the lease.

title: Rent Reporting to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: Tennessee has no rent-reporting program and no rule about requiring tenants to enroll in rent reporting.

title: Sales Tax on Rent
bodyText: Tennessee's landlord-tenant statutes impose no tax on residential rent. Tennessee taxes some lodging and short-term rentals under Title 67; whether a particular residential rent is taxable is a question for the Department of Revenue.

title: Property Tax Statements for Renters
bodyText: Tennessee requires no annual statement of the property-tax portion of rent.

title: Late Fees in Subsidized Housing
bodyText: Tennessee has no separate late-fee rule for subsidized tenants. In the 17 Act counties the 10% cap and five-day grace period apply to all tenants; federal program rules may limit late fees further.

title: Voucher Inspections
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on a landlord's or tenant's refusal of a housing-voucher inspection; federal program rules govern.

title: Subsidy and Rent Abatement
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule on prorating a subsidized tenant's share when rent is abated for habitability problems.

title: Government Shutdowns
bodyText: Tennessee has no rent protection for government workers during a shutdown.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute barring a landlord from passing government fines to a tenant, or limiting it to fines the tenant caused. A pass-through the lease requires is rent in the Act counties; limit it to fines caused by the tenant's conduct.

title: Reimbursing Government Fees
bodyText: No Tennessee statute governs a tenant's reimbursement of government fees (such as registration or inspection fees) the landlord pays. A lease may require it if stated; in the Act counties it is rent.

title: Separately Priced Parking
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule requiring parking to be priced separately from rent.

title: Parking and Towing Rules
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule requiring parking rules to be delivered before signing or limiting mid-lease changes. In the 17 Act counties the Act has its own towing sections for unauthorized and nuisance vehicles; a parking rule adopted after signing binds an Act-county tenant only with reasonable notice and if it does not substantially modify the lease.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule allowing no-notice entry for regularly scheduled services only if the lease says so conspicuously. In the 17 Act counties the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to supply necessary or agreed services, and the landlord may not abuse access; the lease's entry clause sets the notice.

title: Informal Dispute Resolution
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on lease clauses requiring the parties to try informal resolution before suing. A lease may encourage it, but in the 17 Act counties it cannot delay or condition the Act's remedies or notices.

title: Conduct a Tenant Must Avoid
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or let anyone else do so, must not engage in illegal conduct on the premises, and must make sure the tenant and guests do not disturb the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. Outside the Act counties the lease sets these rules.

title: Furnished Rentals
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on furnished rentals or furniture inventories. List furnishings and their condition in the lease.

title: Tenants' Personal Information
bodyText: Tennessee has no landlord-specific rule on disclosing tenant information, except that a landlord may not reveal information that could locate a tenant who ended a lease as a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking. A landlord that holds tenants' computerized personal information must give notice of a security breach under the general identity-theft law.

title: Rent Ledgers and Records
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule requiring a landlord to give a tenant a rent ledger on request or with a notice. Keep a ledger; it is the landlord's proof of the arrearage in a detainer case.

title: Online Portals
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties a landlord may meet the duty to give a maintenance contact by providing an online portal for landlord-tenant communication, and may send notices by email only if the tenant gave an email address in the lease; the landlord may not require an email address. No statute addresses requiring rent payment or signatures through a portal; offer another method.

title: Emergency and Maintenance Contacts
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the landlord must give the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, a telephone number or email address for maintenance services or an online portal, together with the manager's and the owner's or agent's names and addresses, and keep them current. No statute requires a management website or a social-services statement in the lease.

title: Owner Agents for Service
bodyText: In the 17 Act counties the landlord must disclose the name and address of an owner or of a person authorized to accept service of process and notices for the owner. In those counties, a landlord who is not a Tennessee resident, or a corporation not authorized to do business here, may file with the Secretary of State a designation of an in-state agent for service of process; if none is filed, or the agent cannot be served, process may be served on the Secretary of State.

title: Tenant Associations
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute protecting tenants' right to organize or form an association. In the 17 Act counties retaliation is barred only for deposit complaints and use of the Act's remedies.

title: Political Canvassing and Signs
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute giving candidates or canvassers access to apartment buildings or protecting tenants' political signs.

title: Religious Displays
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute giving tenants a right to religious or cultural displays. Rules must be applied without religious discrimination under fair housing law.

title: Home-Based Businesses
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a rental or limiting a lease's restrictions. In the 17 Act counties, unless otherwise agreed, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling.

title: Family Child Care Homes
bodyText: Tennessee does not require a landlord to allow a tenant to run a family child care home. Child care licensing is separate; a lease may restrict business use.

title: Screening Apartment Employees
bodyText: Tennessee does not require background checks for apartment employees.

title: Staff in Senior Housing
bodyText: Tennessee has no work-card or registration rule for staff of 55-and-over housing.

title: Housing Provided to Employees
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a signed disclosure when a landlord houses an employee, or setting how employee housing ends.

title: Student Housing
bodyText: Tennessee has no general exemption for private student housing from landlord-tenant law. The Act does exclude residence at an institution incidental to educational services, and the Human Rights Act allows single-sex dormitory rentals.

title: Veteran Tenant Incentives
bodyText: Tennessee has no landlord incentive or protection program for veteran tenants.

title: Landlord Liability Insurance
bodyText: Tennessee does not require landlords to carry liability insurance or tie it to registration. In the 17 Act counties the landlord must tell the tenant in writing that the landlord does not provide insurance for the tenant's belongings.

title: Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on tenant insurance claims or insurer subrogation against tenants.

title: Prohibited Foreign Parties
bodyText: Tennessee bars a prohibited foreign party, or a business in which it holds a controlling interest, a significant interest (generally 10% or more) or substantial control, from acquiring an interest in agricultural land, and counts a lease of one year or longer (including renewals by option) as an interest; a violator must divest within two years of the finding, and holding such an interest on or after January 1, 2025 is a Class A misdemeanor. A prohibited foreign party includes citizens or residents of listed countries, with exceptions. The statute also defines interests in non-agricultural land, including leases of one year or longer, which later sections address. A landlord leasing agricultural land for a year or more to a person or business connected with a listed country should check the statute first.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: Tennessee makes it a Class B misdemeanor to hunt, trap or fish on another's land without permission of the owner or of the person in charge of the land with the owner's authority. No statute says whether a farm tenant has hunting rights by default; put them in the lease.

title: Tribal or Communal Land
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring government approval of leases of communal or tribal land.

title: Leases by Life Tenants
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute on leases granted by a life tenant or usufructuary.

title: Liens for Tenant Improvements
bodyText: Tennessee's mechanics' lien statutes give liens for work and materials; no lease clause found in the Code keeps a tenant's contractors' liens off the landlord's interest. Require the tenant to get consent before improvements and to keep the property free of liens.

title: Eminent Domain and Rent
bodyText: No Tennessee statute found says whether a residential tenant's rent ends or shrinks when the property is taken by eminent domain. Say in the lease that the lease ends on a taking and how any award is shared.

title: Foreclosure Disclosure
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose a pending foreclosure to tenants; federal law protects some tenants after foreclosure.

title: Notice of Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to notify tenants of foreclosure, condemnation or other adverse proceedings, or requiring tenants to forward notices; the library's clause asks the tenant to forward them.

title: Leases Void for Illegal Use
bodyText: Tennessee declares unenforceable any lease of premises used to sell, display or exhibit obscene material or performances, and a tenancy may be terminated where the premises or the area immediately around them is knowingly used for listed drug or prostitution offenses. Other illegal use is a lease breach (and in the Act counties a breach of the tenant's duty not to engage in illegal conduct).

title: Nuisance Abatement
bodyText: A nonprofit, the city or county, the owner or legal occupant of a parcel adversely affected by the building's condition, or an interested person such as a lienholder may petition a court to declare a building a public nuisance (including one no longer fit and habitable); if neither the owner nor an interested person abates it, the court may appoint a receiver whose lien comes ahead of prior mortgages (see the receivership row). A general nuisance-abatement statute also exists. In the 17 Act counties the Act lets a landlord tow nuisance vehicles. A lease cannot prevent these proceedings.

title: Code Enforcement and Receivership
bodyText: Tennessee lets a nonprofit, the city or county, the owner or legal occupant of a parcel adversely affected by the building's condition, or an interested person such as a lienholder petition a court in rem to have a building declared a public nuisance (including one no longer fit and habitable). Filing creates a receiver's lien that is a first lien ahead of earlier and later liens, including mortgages. If a certificate of public nuisance is attached to the petition, the filing also bars transfers, including by foreclosure, until the petition is dismissed or the court authorizes a transfer. If neither the owner nor an interested person allowed to do the work abates the nuisance, the court may appoint a receiver to take possession and control. The chapter does not itself mention rents, but it gives the receiver the powers of a tax-enforcement receiver under § 67-5-2103.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute stopping cities from restricting accessory dwelling units or addressing their rental. A separate statute lets a temporary family healthcare structure be a permitted accessory use subject to local accessory-dwelling requirements.

title: Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute limiting rentals in single-family zones to owner-occupied lots. Local zoning may apply; associations may not retroactively ban long-term rentals of single-family homes against existing owners.

title: Health Department Rental Rules
bodyText: Tennessee has no statute requiring a landlord to provide health-district rental regulations or refer tenants to the health department.

title: Health Code Variances
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule requiring a health-code variance for a rental to be given to tenants or attached to the lease.

title: Outstanding Code Orders
bodyText: Tennessee does not require a landlord to disclose outstanding inspection or condemnation orders to tenants.

title: Penalties for Inspection Entry
bodyText: Tennessee sets no penalty for a landlord's inspection entry beyond the Act's remedies for abusive entry in the 17 Act counties (injunction, actual damages and fees).

title: Repair Escrow Exemption Notices
bodyText: Tennessee has no rent-escrow remedy, so no exemption notice applies.

title: Single-Family Occupancy Disclosures
bodyText: Tennessee has no single-family rental occupancy disclosure with font-size or first-page placement rules.

title: Small-Landlord Exemptions
bodyText: Tennessee's landlord-tenant act has no small-portfolio exemption; it applies by county population, with listed exclusions (institutions, contract-of-sale occupancy, transient lodging, condominium and cooperative owners, agricultural premises). The Human Rights Act exempts an owner-occupied building of no more than two families.

title: Tenants and Special Districts
bodyText: Tennessee gives tenants no representation or voting rule in utility or improvement districts.

title: Tenant Protection Act Exemption Notices
bodyText: Tennessee has no tenant protection act with rent or just-cause limits, so there is no exemption notice. Local rent control is barred.

title: Tenant Protection Act Notices
bodyText: Tennessee has no tenant protection act notice.

title: Sunset of Tenant Protections
bodyText: Tennessee's core landlord-tenant statutes have no repeal date; the Act's county list is fixed by the 2010 census.

title: Common-Area Electricity
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule on making a tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's meter. In the 17 Act counties the landlord must keep common areas clean and safe; disclose any such wiring and price it in the lease.

title: After a Disaster
bodyText: Tennessee has no separate disaster rule for tenancies. In the 17 Act counties a fire or other casualty that substantially impairs the unit (deemed unfit for human habitation by a governmental authority) lets the tenant vacate and end the lease, with rent accounted to the vacating date and prepaid rent and deposit returned; if restoration requires the tenant to leave, the landlord may end the lease on 14 days' notice. Outside the Act counties a tenant who was not at fault may surrender an untenantable building and owe no later rent unless a written agreement says otherwise.

title: Hosting Displaced Guests
bodyText: Tennessee has no rule letting tenants host people displaced by a disaster despite lease guest limits.

title: Environmental Events
bodyText: Tennessee gives no landlord or tenant termination right for environmental events beyond the casualty rules. A landlord's opt-in right would have to be in the lease, and in the 17 Act counties it cannot cut the tenant's casualty rights.

title: When a Defect Is Serious Enough
bodyText: Tennessee's Act ties the landlord's code duty to requirements 'materially affecting health and safety', defines essential services as utility services such as gas, heat and electricity plus other landlord obligations that materially affect health and safety, and lets the tenant end the lease after a casualty that substantially impairs the unit, which it defines as the unit being deemed unfit for human habitation by a governmental authority. It has no other materiality test for habitability defects.

title: Presumptions About Habitability
bodyText: Tennessee has no statutory presumption that a unit is or is not habitable.

title: Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: Tennessee does not require the lease to state that the landlord will deliver the unit fit for habitation. In the 17 Act counties the duty applies by statute anyway.

title: Habitability Rules Tennessee Does Not Have
bodyText: Tennessee has no statutory habitability duty outside the 17 Act counties, no rent escrow or clerk deposit, no general repair-and-deduct, no rent-reduction-for-conditions rule, no habitability presumption, no minimum heat, water-heater, window-guard, pool-barrier, balcony or bed-bug statute, and no statement of habitability in the lease. Each absence has its own row with its search battery.

title: Other Rules Tennessee Does Not Have
bodyText: Tennessee has no just-cause eviction, rent control (local control is barred), rent-increase notice, deposit cap, application-fee cap, lease-copy duty, plain-language or translation rule, tenant-rights guide, tenant-organizing protection, rent-reporting, smart-lock or security-device statute. Each absence has its own row with its search battery.

title: Related Rules Outside the Landlord-Tenant Title
bodyText: Some Tennessee rules that affect landlords sit outside Title 66: the unauthorized-occupant (squatter) removal procedure in the detainer chapter, smoke-alarm duties in the fire-safety titles, the Non-Smoker Protection Act, the service-animal misrepresentation offense, the sex-offender residence limits, the Human Rights Act's housing rules, and the homestead and personal-property exemptions.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Tennessee follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Tennessee's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the act, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-516). The act applies only in the 17 counties listed in Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-102(a): Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson. Elsewhere in Tennessee, the landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith, and whether courts imply a covenant of good faith and fair dealing in a lease is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
